title: The river passes
hookLine: Confucius stands by a river and says it flows on like this, day and night (Analects 9.16)

cards: Have you ever stood on a bridge and watched the water go under? It's oddly hard to walk away from. The water you're looking at is gone before you've finished looking, and yet the river stays exactly where it is.
Kids stare at it. Old people stare at it. Nobody has to explain why.
In China, long ago, a teacher stood by a stream and said one short sentence. Readers still argue about what he meant.

teach.b: The teacher is Confucius, and the sentence is in the Analects, the collection of his sayings that, tradition says, his students gathered.
In James Legge's old translation, it reads: "The Master standing by a stream, said, 'It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!'" That's the whole passage. No explanation, no moral.
And because he didn't explain, readers hear two very different things in it.
Some hear a sigh: time running away like water, day and night, and us getting older on the bank.
Tradition remembers Confucius as a teacher who spent long years hoping a ruler would put his teaching to use; heard that way, it's gentle grief about time. Others hear encouragement.
The river doesn't rest on its good days or quit on its bad ones. It keeps going, and over years it cuts through rock.
Mencius, yesterday's teacher, praised water that comes from a real spring, because it flows on day and night and fills every hollow before moving on.
Some later Confucian readers heard in the river the ceaseless working of the world itself. You don't have to choose; maybe both are true at once.
Time does pass, and the way to meet passing time is to keep flowing with it, a little each day.
In Greece, Plato reports the philosopher Heraclitus saying you can't step into the same river twice.
Two thinkers, far apart, both watching water.

how: The line from the Analects is often quoted in Chinese when people speak of passing time, and readers take it as a lament, a call to steady effort, or both.

games.q: you're standing with Confucius by a stream. he watches the water, then speaks. what does he say?
o: a river teaches us to rule a kingdom
it passes on like this, not ceasing day or night
let us cross before it rises
games.why: it passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night. that's all he says, and people still debate whether it's a sigh or a push.

practice: If you're near a river, a fountain, rain, or a tap you can run slowly, watch it; if not, pour a glass and watch the surface settle, or picture a stream you've known.
Watch the water arrive and leave without trying to hold any of it. Notice your breath doing the same, in and out, never the same breath twice: just like this.

wordCard.voice: Confucius. His one sentence at the stream: it goes on like this, day and night. A sigh, or a push, or both.
